utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, this is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic can wait for a second. He should --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He doesn't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any technical problem but no time for consultation after this delay of half an hour, Mr. Stojanovic, because I will say something about it. Informally, the Chamber received the following report about the late arrival of Mr. Mladic. The transport police team leader indicated that Mr. Mladic did not agree with the starting time of 9.00 today. Furthermore, he would have indicated that he does not want to arrive half an hour before his trial starts. Therefore, this morning he was not ready to depart the UNDU when the transport police arrived. Mr. Stojanovic, let one thing be very clear, unless there is a motion by the Defence, which of course we'll deal with, Mr. Mladic should be ready to come to the premises of this Tribunal at the time as determined by this Chamber. If Mr. Mladic considers it too early, it's fine. Not being ready will be considered by this Chamber as a clear and explicit waiver to be present at his trial. Therefore, if we get a similar report tomorrow, we'll just start and at the first break, Mr. Mladic will have an opportunity to join us, and that he misses the first part in court is his problem. It is the result of a waiver of his right to be present at trial. Let that be clear. I'm not going to spend any further words on it. It would be a further waste of time. No loud speaking, no loud speaking. Mr. Mladic, you have caused already sufficient delay today. You have -- unless necessary at this moment for urgent matters, you have an opportunity to speak to counsel during the break. Then I have to correct myself, I earlier said that we expected Judge Fluegge to be back tomorrow. That will be the day after tomorrow. It also means that the absence of Judge Fluegge for urgent personal reasons will not be longer than the five days provided for in the Rules, five working days. Then if the Defence is ready to call its next witness, Mr. Stojanovic, you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Could we kindly call Witness Zoran Durmic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honour, good morning. I would like to introduce Mr. Jonathan MacDonald, who will be representing the Office of the Prosecution and he will be cross-examining the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for introducing Mr. MacDonald, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Durmic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, I'd like to invite you to make the solemn declaration for which the text is now handed out to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Durmic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Durmic, you will first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You find him to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Durmic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you for the record and slowly to tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Durmic. I was born on the 15th of October, 1960.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell the Chamber whether at one time, you gave a statement, a written statement to the Defence team of Radovan Karadzic for the trial of Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please have in e-court document under 65 ter 1D04284.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Durmic, can you see in front of you the statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On this last page, do you see the signature and the date, 12th February, 2013?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature and is this the date that you put in yourself?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you this, during preparations for your appearance here in this courtroom --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we, before that, look at paragraph 27 of this witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: -- did you indicate in paragraph 27 that it was necessary in the second sentence to add the word "nearly," and then the text would go on to read, "Nearly all Serbian villages were burned to the ground."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And let us now look at paragraph 40 of your statement. Did you suggest to me that the meaning of your answers would have been different if a correction would be made so that after the word, "there were no killings of the Muslims captives" there would be a full stop and then it should go on to say "According to what I heard from my colleagues when I revisited the location," and then the text would go on to read: "They were taken somewhere by buses, I think to Bratunac or Zvornik."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, today, after you have made these two corrections, would you give the same answers to the same questions after you have made a solemn declaration and are these questions and answers, or rather, the latter given to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now is the time for me to ask this statement of Durmic Zoran to be admitted into evidence which is marked 1D04284.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D4284 receives number D659, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D659 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, I'm going to read the summary of this witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Before the outbreak of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Zoran Durmic was deployed with the reserve police force of the Vlasenica SJB in the police station in Milici MUP.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, we don't have the summary in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, have you distributed the summary in English to the booth? You say yes, but the booth reports to me that they have not received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I distributed only a B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you then please read slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. He testifies about the interethnic incidents, that the -- he processed as a criminal investigator. He highlighted one of the events when he and his colleagues were disarmed and detained. He says that he knows that the Muslims were speedily arming themselves and preparing for war by obtaining and acquiring weapons which was spearheaded by the commander of the Vlasenica SJB, the leadership of the SDA, and the leader of the religious community in Vlasenica. In discharging his professional duties, he is aware of an attack made by the Muslims on the 21st of May, 1992, in the area of Zutica village when they killed nine Serbian workers, as well as about the incident of 27th of May, 1992, where in the area of Konjevic Polje, five drivers of the bauxite mine were killed in an ambush and the company lorry was set alight. Then, this was followed by attacks on the Serbian villages on a daily basis, the expulsion of the population and the looting of their property. He also spoke about what he knew about the tragic events of the 16th of May, 1992, in the village of Zaklopaca when several Muslims were killed. He emphasised that this was not a planned or an organised action whatsoever. Commenting the documents, he gave information about the treatment of the captured deputy commander of the Srpska detachment in relation to his exchange. Finally, he speaks about his direct tasks and his perception of the situation along the Milici-Djugum road on 13th of July, 1992 [as interpreted], and on the situation on that same day on the football playground in Kasaba where he saw a large group of Muslim captives. That would be the summary of the statement. I would kindly ask that on page 7, line 12 of the transcript, it should read 13th of July, 1995 instead of 1992. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Durmic, I would like to ask you a few questions. Let us look at paragraph 27 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for the transcript and for the record it bears the mark of D659.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In it, you speak --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't understand what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You will get it in a moment. Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say after the correction that we made today that nearly all the Serbian villages were burned to the ground, can you be specific and tell the Chamber which villages in your area were burned by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: These are the villages of Valcici [phoen], Metaljka, Vuksici, Bukovica, Erici, Vasiljevici, part of Visnjica, Rupovo Brdo, Podravanje where about 30 residents perished, then the open pit bauxite mine, Milici-Bracan where eight guards were killed, two were found totally charred and three were ran over by a tank. That was the most atrocious crime that I saw in my whole career in the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 34 of your statement, D659, you speak about a document and a letter in the drafting of which you participated as well with a view to stopping the exchange of Mirsad Sulejmanovic who at the time was the deputy commander of the Cer platoon. Will you please tell the Chamber more specifically whether you know what was the final outcome in the case of Mirsad Sulejmanovic and whether the exchange was carried out of him as member of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: In front of Milici public security station on behalf of the station, we sent a letter to the staff and the commission for the exchange and the Sarajevo security services centre that was our superior to the effect that Mirsad Sulejmanovic was the deputy of the Cer detachment, not the platoon as you stated. Every day, they were launching attacks on the Serbian villages that I listed a while ago, and we requested that this exchange be halted, that this person should be processed before competent courts. However, they proceeded with the exchange, most probably because that was in the better interest because he was exchanged for a large number of Serbs. This person still lives somewhere in the United States or in Canada because I saw him some time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 38 of your statement, you speak about the events of 1995 and you say that at one point, you and your unit occupied the road and that on that occasion, on the playground, football playground in Kasaba you saw a large group of Muslims who were guarded by soldiers of our army. Let me first ask you this, can you be more specific and tell the Chamber when exactly was that when you were passing by the football playground in Kasaba and I mean which part of the day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was between 12.00 and 1.00 but I think that was closer to the noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My second question is when you say you saw a large group of Muslims, could you please tell the Chamber in your view, what is a large group of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Well, according to my visual assessment, I might say that there were approximately 100 men. I don't think there were more than that. They might have even been fewer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were these people standing, sitting on the ground, lying on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you exactly. Some of them were sitting, some were lying. It was in the part of the playground closer to the main road so I was some 50 or 60 metres away. So if you take into account the size of the playground and my view, I saw a few lads whom I didn't know who were wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The deployment of your unit along the Milici-Djugum road, where exactly were your soldiers and how far were they from the playground?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: This was not exactly a police unit. It was just a number of police officers who had already been deployed in that area. I joined them the following day because I had bereavement in my family so on the date when I arrived there around 12.00 noon, I found them in the area of Djugum. In my opinion this is some 300 or 400 metres away from the playground but there is a curve that blocks the view of the playground and one cannot see the situation there. We held about 200 metres of this road, a section of 200 or 300 metres, I cannot tell you exactly but we did occupy the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the next paragraph, number 39, you speak about an incident that you yourself witnessed when one of the wounded Muslims said that Zulfo Tursunovic had wounded him in Bokcin Potok, that he had killed the brother and many others who had intended to surrender. Can you tell me where did this happen exactly, can you briefly tell the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Well, that happened when I was going to join the police that was already deployed on the road in order to give them certain instructions and to see whether they needed food. While I was driving in a car along the main road, I recognised medical staff from the regional hospital Milici and Dr. Sveto who was taking care of someone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please slow down. The interpreters have difficulties following you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will. So when I arrived in the vehicle on the left-hand side, in the upper right-hand corner of the playground, near the corner, I saw an ambulance and ambulance crew. I recognised the medical staff from the Milici regional hospital, Dr. Sveto Marinkovic or Svetozar Marinkovic was among them. I stopped there and I asked the doctor who's been wounded. I was afraid that it might have been some of the policemen or one of the policemen. He said no, they were taking the wounded Muslims out. I got out of the car, I greeted him and I saw a middle-aged man who was being offered medical assistance. He was on his left-hand side. He was lying on his left side and I noticed that there was an entry wound. [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We don't receive translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apology, the microphone was off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The nurse was offering him treatment and asked him, Where were you wounded. He said, Go to Bokcin Potok.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed with your next question. Or before we continue, could I ask you one clarifying question. When you are saying the upper right-hand corner of the playground near the corner, are you talking about the Kasaba football pitch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. I was looking at it from the direction of Milici, that's the direction that I was coming from. So that's why I said the upper right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I will conclude with this question. Mr. Durmic, could you explain for the benefit of the Court, how long did you stay in that area when you arrived there and where did you return to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Well, I stayed there for about ten minutes and I then continued in the direction of Djugum which is where I met this police officers who had already been deployed there. I really don't know who deployed them there but I was told that I should convey them the task they had. They had to secure the road and ensure that it was not cut off or that it didn't come under threat. Traffic should be able to pass through unhindered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And having completed that task, did you return from that sector?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Afterwards, I returned to the police in Milici. I didn't linger at the playground, I went on to the Milici police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please just inform the Court of the following when the wounded man said -- when the Muslim said go to Bokcin Potok, could you tell the Court, because it's difficult for us to see where that is, could you tell the Court where Bokcin Potok is actually located?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I've never been there. It's in the Bratunac area, in the municipality of Bratunac. I think it's between Buljim and Kravica. As far as I know it would be somewhere in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the direction that the 28th Division of the BH army was heading in?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honour, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. I've been told the full sentence hasn't been recorded when you interrupted because the court wasn't receiving any interpretation. What did that wounded member, Muslim member say when the nurse was treating his wound, she asked him where were you wounded and he said well, you should go to Bokcin Potok, 1.000 people who were dead there, the son of Zulfo killed us and she said how.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: He cursed our refugee mothers because we wanted to surrender and he wouldn't allow this. And then she asked him, Where are you from if you're a refugee? He said, I'm from Didici [phoen], and he continued crying out and he said oh my dear mother, he's killed my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And after this amendment has been made in paragraph 40, could you tell us the following, at what time of day or at what time in the evening when you went to that section of the road again, what time of day or what time of the evening was it when you went to that road?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: It was not quite dark. It was dusk, I would say. I went there -- I was told the policemen would spend the night there so I took them some canvasses, some tents so that they didn't have to sleep out in the open. It was summertime so it could have been half past 8.00 or 9.00, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Durmic. I just wanted to complete your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now, Your Honour, I would now like to tender the documents that we have used with this witness or for this witness. There are six such documents. Can I read them all out or should I go one by one? 1D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first try to find out whether there will be any objections because if so, then we will take them one by one. If not, you can read them all six immediately. Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution only objected to one associated exhibit. I discussed this with my friend prior to the witness's examination in chief and I understand he's not going to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So whatever the witness -- what Mr. Stojanovic will tender there are no objections. Then you can read them in one round, Mr. Stojanovic. So if you read the five numbers then Madam Registrar will in the same sequence will assign numbers to them and the Chamber will decide on admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I'd like to tender the following documents: 65 ter documents 1D04285, and then 1D04286, 1D04287, and 1D04288. As my young colleague said, in that case, we won't tender the last document on the list, 1D04287 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the six from become five and one of the five will not be tendered. That makes four all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I understand the transcript and the interpretation recorded the one not to be tendered as 04287. I believe that should be 04289, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, otherwise there will be one document which you do and do not tender at the same time. Is the correction made by Mr. MacDonald accurate?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's correct. I think the number is correct. Let me just be quite sure. It's only the last one, 04289 that I won't be tendering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, 1D04285 through 88 would receive numbers ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Numbers D660 up and including D663, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D660 up and including D663 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one question for the witness before we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, in your statement you said that the wounded men who addressed you said, He killed my brother and many others. Today, you make that -- you mentioned a number of a thousand. What's -- what happened that where earlier "many" were mentioned it's now a thousand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could I clarify this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking you to tell me what happened that your testimony in this respect developed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm quoting the wounded Muslim who was being given medical assistance. He wasn't talking to me. He was talking to the medical staff and this is what I heard, of course I was at a distance of two or three metres from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, that's not the issue for me whether he addressed the nurses or whether he addressed you. But earlier, you stated that he would have said that many were killed or that -- yes, he killed my brother and many others, whereas today you come with a number of thousand. What happened in that your statement that we find "many" and what is it that today you tell us that he said "thousand".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What he said was, Go to Bokcin Potok, thousands have been killed there or there are a thousand dead there, perhaps there was a typo, something was perhaps misprinted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, in your statement, the statement you signed -- you confirmed, you would have said, "He killed my brother and many others. And then as far as Bokcin Potok is concerned you said there are masses of dead people without giving a number and today you give us a number of a thousand. What happened that today it's a thousand and earlier it was masses or many? What happened that you suddenly come up with the number of a thousand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing in particular. I quite simply remembered what was said. There were many dead. Well, that means that the number was a large number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Many dead doesn't mean that it's a large number but in itself -- but apparently since you confirmed your statement where you made small corrections, you now since half an hour ago, you remember that a thousand was mentioned by this man.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, very well, let it be a large number as I said in this statement. It wasn't my intention to obstruct these proceedings in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No it's not about obstructing. What I would like to know is what the man said. And what explains the different versions of what you tell us the man had said. What did he say, did he say a thousand or did he say many or did he say masses or what did he say? If you don't remember, just tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He said that a mass of people had been killed in Bokcin Potok, a large number of people, Zulfo and his henchmen had done this because they had decided to surrender and he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That part is clear so the thousand of today was just a conclusion you translated a mass of people in being a thousand. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps this was a personal conclusion that I drew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. MacDonald, we have still ten minutes until the break. Are you ready to start your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Durmic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. MacDonald. Mr. MacDonald is counsel for the Prosecution. You find him to your right. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, after you were called up to the Milici police office in February or March 1992, did you continue to work there throughout the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: I was called up on the 22nd of September, 1991 pursuant to an order from Mr. Delimustafic, the Ministry of the Interior --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If I can just stop you there, Witness. I appreciate you were called up in 1991. I understand you then went to back to work and were called up once again in February or March of 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. In February or March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Did you continue to work from that time throughout the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes. You mean in the police force?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. Did you continue to work in the police force?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Is it correct that the police station in Milici became an SJB around mid-May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: I don't know of the exact date but after the municipality of Milici had been established, I believe that an SJB public security station was established. It was in the second half of May, 1992, I think, but I'm not certain. I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Is it correct that Radomir Bjelanovic became the chief of SJB Milici when SJB Milici was established?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And did Radomir Bjelanovic and SJB Milici report to CSB Sarajevo and its chief, Zoran Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: The Milici SJB was under the Sarajevo CSB. As to whether Zoran Cvijetic was the chief of the CSB at the time, I'm not sure. I'm not sure that that was the case from the outset. He was the chief at one point in time but I don't know whether it was from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Turning to SJB Milici, Witness, were there duty officers who worked there on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes, as in the case of all other SJBs, it did have a duty roster, it did have duty officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that the task of the duty officer was to record the significant events of any one day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what the task was. If citizens wanted to have a record made of any -- of anything that had changed, the details would be taken down by those who were working the relevant shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: How many police officers worked at SJB Milici when it was first established, Witness?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say what the exact number was. At the time, I was still a reserve policeman. I don't know the exact number of those employed at the time because there were five or six criminal policemen in the police station, they were maintained there and later others joined but I don't know the exact numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying the number changed from day to day as police officers went to aid the army?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Well, that's quite possible, depending on the situation on the ground, on how complex the situation was in the territory of the municipality. The numbers probably changed, as I said. I'm not quite sure when it comes to the numbers of employees in the SJB.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: With regard to police officers going to help the army, do you know how the army communicated with the SJB on how many numbers it needed on a day-to-day basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. I believe it would be necessary to specify the period concerned for such a vague question. Which period does this question relate to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald, did you have any specific period in mind or did you mean the whole of the time the witness served in Milici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, I can specify it to May and June of 1992 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you then please repeat the question with this specification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, with regard to police officers going to help the army, in May and June of 1992, do you know how the army communicated with the SJB regarding how many police officers it needed on a day-to-day basis?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. This concerned the chief and the commander. It wasn't within my purview. I wasn't there. I don't know how they communicated, how this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I wonder if this point the Prosecution could have 65 ter number 10705, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think when it's brought to our screens, we might also -- unless you can finish it in one or two questions, otherwise I would deal with the matter after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I do only have one or two questions on this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll listen to the answers of these limited number of questions then take the break afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, on the first page in the heading, we see that this is a report being sent to a Mr. Zoran Cvijetic at CSB Sarajevo dated the 3rd of August in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And if we can move to the last page in both documents. That's page 2 in the B/C/S and 4 in the English. I believe we need the next page in the English if possible, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, I'm right in saying this is being sent by Radomir Bjelanovic, the chief of Milici SJB who was your chief at the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can we please stay on the second page in the B/C/S and page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, if I can take you to the paragraph beginning paragraph B. In the English it is at the top of the page, in the B/C/S, about halfway down. This paragraph, the first few lines describe a number of policemen and that they were engaged in combat activity in May, June and July of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: This report was drafted by the chief of the public security station. This is the first time that I'm seeing this document and I really cannot comment on what he has written.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Very well. One final question then. The last paragraph before the letter C on the page, the first line states: "There were no problems with regards the cooperation and command." In your experience, Witness, is it accurate to say there were no problems with regard to cooperation and command?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what he meant. I personally didn't have any problems. Now, what he understood to be problems, I really cannot comment. This letter being authored by him, I don't know what kind of reports he sent and what he did in general. Believe me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. But you personally didn't have any problem with regards to cooperation and command between the army and the police?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what the witness said, I think, Mr. MacDonald. Before we take the break, could I ask you one additional question, Witness. This report apart from the fact that you've never seen it before, describes that six times in May with about 30 policemen, the police station was engaged in combat activity. Does this ring a bell to you that for such a number of days in the month of May, 30 policemen were engaged in combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, he might have inferred here that the overall engagement was about 30, when you put them all together, not on each occasion. As for combat activities, the major problem that the police had was to secure the Milici mine road because this road had been constantly cut off by Muslim formations. They were taking prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So apparently you have some knowledge about members of the police station being engaged in combat activities and you're describing them now in a bit further detail. Were you, yourself, ever engaged in combat activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'd like to tell you is that the number of 30 policemen might mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, what I'd like you to do is to answer my question. Were you, yourself, ever engaged in combat activities being sent from the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What kind of combat activities were you engaged in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were involved in providing security of the road just like in the incident when the bus with passengers was captured at the bauxite mine. On another occasion, our patrol was captured which necessitated for us to secure the road between Milici and the bauxite mine because more than 25 employees of the mine had been killed on that road on their way from or to work. We were even involved in loading and unloading the bauxite ore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You never were engaged -- did your engagement lead to any exchange of fire with Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I personally I cannot remember. Not me personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. We'll take a break after the witness has left the courtroom. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, in your summary, you said something about the witness emphasising that a certain action in which Muslims were killed was not organised, et cetera. The only thing I read, apart from that the incident is not described in any further detail, that it was part of combat. It didn't say anything else so therefore I had some difficulties in following you in that summary but I leave it to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. That's paragraph 30 and 31 of the witness statement where he provides more details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that in 31 there is more emphasis on nobody had planned it. What exactly happened is still pretty unclear from both paragraph 30 and paragraph 31 but we have to live with that. Mr. MacDonald, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I do, the Prosecution would seek to tender the document we were discussing just before the break, that is 65 ter 10705.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 10705 receives number P6792, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, I would now like to turn to a new topic. With regard to Vlasenica municipality, do you know roughly the percentages of Muslims and Serbs in that municipality in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald, it's recorded on the transcript your question doesn't mention the name of the municipality, would you like to mention that please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was referring to Vlasenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One additional question, Mr. MacDonald. Did you seek to establish the awareness of the witness or did you seek to establish the numerical strength of the various ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I was seeking to establish the numerical strength of the ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Typically a matter to agree upon with the defence. I mean 1991 census is there so if you want to establish that, I could not -- I would imagine that there would be no dispute about that. Could you please keep that in mind for any other matters. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: One last question, Witness, with regards to an ethnic breakdown. Are you aware of whether Zaklopaca was a predominantly Muslim or Serbian village in 1991 before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: It was a mixed village. Zaklopaca itself, one part of the population was Muslim, whereas the villages closer to Zaklopaca were populated by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, at the start of the cross-examination, you mentioned that Milici municipality was established and at that time SJB Milici was also established. Are you aware of when the municipality of Vlasenica was divided and Milici municipality was established from that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have 65 ter 02894 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you'll see from the screen this is a protocol on the agreement of the territorial partition of Vlasenica municipality. I'm not going to ask you with regards to the verification of this document but I would like to ask you one question regarding something contained within it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can we please have page 6 in the B/C/S and page 4 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, at the top of your page, the very first paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And for the benefit of Your Honours, the very last paragraph in the English --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: -- am I right in saying that it reads, "According to the principle of ethnicity, certain settlements including Zaklopaca, the Muslim part, should be part of the Muslim municipality of Vlasenica." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: I can see it in this document but as a matter of fact, I am not able to comment on this document. This was done and drafted by politicians and I don't know exactly who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please now have 65 ter 31350.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald, I don't know what your question would have been if the witness would not have said that he cannot comment on anything politicians have created, which, by of way, of course, doesn't prevent you asking questions about what happened. I have no idea what you had on your mind but apparently the effect that the witness cannot comment on something created by politicians seems to keep you from asking any further questions, which makes me curious to know what you would have asked. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I hope to proceed with this line of questioning nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: With regard to this document, Witness, this is a decision to create an assembly of the Serbian people in the municipality of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And if we can scroll down to the bottom in both documents. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If I can take you to point 2 of this document, and I believe in the English it's roughly eight lines down, and the B/C/S, roughly ten lines down. The area of the Serbian municipality of Vlasenica will include -- and do you see the village Zaklopaca there, Witness?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Which line?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I believe it's line ten in the B/C/S, although I must admit, my B/C/S is far from perfect.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And am I right in saying, Witness, that in this document, there is no differentiation between the Muslim part and the Serbian part, it is the entire village that is included.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: As I told you, this document and these political decisions is really something that I am unable to comment. The people who drafted this or who had this meeting are better placed to comment on this and they would probably paint a better picture for you of the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I wonder then if we can remain on this topic here, Witness, and turn to the day of the 16th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I wonder if we can bring the witness's statement up on to the screen, that's D659, and look at paragraph 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald, that previous document, the decision, is there any date known for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that document is undated in our collection, Your Honour, but I believe there is a witness coming with whom we could explore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we hear from that witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, in paragraph 30, the first thing I would like to clarify you speak about being at Opetci where the Muslims attacked and you describe it as an exceptionally strong Muslim attack, the fighting went on for several hours. For the sake of clarity, Witness, can you explain how that accords with the fact you don't recall being in combat with the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: On that day, the 16th of May, the road was being unblocked and I can show you that on the map, that's a regional road between Milici and Zeleni Jadar in the village of Zutica. The road passes along the Jadar river valley, the territorial forces were engaged in fierce fighting with paramilitary Muslim forces who had cut off the road and they were pushed towards the village of Opetci. The task of the police was to occupy the free area so that from certain points we would be able to check this road in order to avoid the repetition of what had happened earlier. I told you that we lost more than 20 people on their way to work. However, there was fierce fighting up there. The Muslims broke through the line, pushed the territorial forces, penetrated the territory in depth and the result was a total mayhem. These people returned to Milici at around 10.00 in the evening and we arrive in the evening hours. During that attack and this fighting, four persons were killed. Among them was one of my colleagues from the bauxite mine where I used to work. He was a member of the Brkic family and I heard that it had occurred in Zaklopaca. Let me clarify. When you view it from the town of Milic -- Zutica is -- very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Zaklopaca in a moment. You speak about the Muslims breaking through the line. Did you engage in combat with the Muslim forces at any time, you personally.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: We were in this liberated part of the territory as I said a while ago. I said if we had had a map, I could have explained to you the situation on the ground. The task of the police was to control the road from various points because this road passes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the simple question is whether you personally were engaged in combat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were not personally involved in any shooting or fighting. We did not clash there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's an answer to the question. Next question, please, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Turning to the events of Zaklopaca on the same day, are you aware that around 80 people were killed in that attack and that they were exclusively Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't know that evening that so many people were killed. I still don't know the exact number. But when I arrived to the bereaving family in the evening, somebody said that somebody had done this in Zaklopaca. This is all the information that I have relating to Zaklopaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Very well. So you're not aware that the next day, a group of 30 women, children and one elderly man that survived what took place at Zaklopaca, they walked to Vlasenica, surrendered to Serb soldiers, had to sign statements saying they were giving their houses and properties to the Serbs, and were then bused to a place near to Kladanj. You're not aware of that course of events?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. This is the first time I'm hearing about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Do you know someone called Milomir Milosevic, Witness?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was my fellow police officer from the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And was he a member of the Milici SJB in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was an active-duty policeman. He had been working at the station for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Are you aware that a survivor of the incident at Zaklopaca stated that they saw Milomir Milosevic arrive in a police car at Zaklopaca on the 16th of May, 1992, along with other armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I wonder if at this point the Prosecution could have 65 ter 02856, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While waiting for that, could I ask you the following question: In your statement you say that a number of Muslims were killed in Zaklopaca. Do you know whether these were combatants or civilians or do you have any knowledge about their status?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, the document on the screen in front of you is a duty report sent by the duty officer Milan Bacic on the 16th of May 1992 to the commander of the police station in Milici. It's stated he took over duty at 7.00. If I could take you to the part marked patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And Your Honours, I would refer to a quotation from the B/C/S document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm correct in saying that the duty officer states: "All personnel were engaged in and I quote "ciscenja terena".

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: The term "cleaning of the ground" is something that he probably referred to as engagement of Zutica. The proper formulation should be the search of the ground following a certain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you were asked whether you agree with Mr. MacDonald that that is the wording used, not -- you were not asked whether it's correct or not, just to establish what the document says for the time being.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what the report says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution would now request to have 65 ter 02857 on the screen. And Your Honours, this document that is arriving is linked to the one we've just discussed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, this is a report again by the duty officer, Milan Bacic. We're still on the 16th of May. He states he took over at 3.00 and he's passing on duty at 11.00. If I can again take you to the part parked "patrol," he again states "All personnel are still engaged in 'ciscenja terena'". That is what he is reporting to the commander of Milici police station; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, if I may notice the following, this report was made on the same day. He says I took over the duty at 0700. However, I see here that he says it took place at 0500 hours. I cannot understand and I don't know how to comment to reports written by the same person stating different hours. He said that I took over the duty at 7.00 and in the next one, it says I took over the duty at 0500 in correct order and I pass it on to the next duty officer in correct state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, if there were any questions to relation to that in re-examination, questions may be asked to you. You're not here to tell us what you consider to be adequate or not, you're here to answer questions and the question was whether you agree with Mr. MacDonald that the same language is used in this document as in the previous one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question, please, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, my final question, do you agree with me that these duty reports are written on the same day of the incident at Zaklopaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: I agree that they were written on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my cross-examination. I would request to tender the last two documents that the Prosecution has used, 65 ter 2856 and 2857, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2856 receives number P6793 and document 2857 receives number P6794, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both are admitted into evidence. Mr. MacDonald, you only asked the witness to confirm what the language is which is used in those documents and then whether they're of the same date. If you would have had no witness, I would have been in a position to answer those questions. Therefore, it's a bit unclear to me -- because the witness wanted to explain something and of course I do not know what he wants to explain but it would have been -- I do not fully understand why you asked the questions everyone who can read can answer and then leave all other possible questions out. But perhaps Mr. Stojanovic has questions in relation to this. Mr. Stojanovic, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us try to clarify this, Your Honours. Let us first look at document P6794.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would attempt to simply clarify the timing of this document. In the B/C/S version, if you have it in front of you, in the heading, it says --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Are we talking about the same document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It says on the 16th of May, 1992, I received the duty -- but it says zero then something was typed over the zero and then it says 5 hours. Now looking at the B/C/S version, would you be able to say that this is actually at 0500 hours or at 1500 hours?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Well, it is impossible. If the previous one, he had taken over the duty at 0700 hours, why would he take over the duty then on the 1500 hours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is whether you read this to be 05 or 15, Mr. Stojanovic, isn't it? Could you answer that question? Irrespective Mr. Stojanovic, whether it's the witness that should answer that question or whether the Chamber that should answer that question looking at the original. But if the witness wants to express himself whether it's 15 or 05, apart from logic, how do you read it, 05 or 15, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's both in my opinion, both 05 and 15. If I could say something else --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, I have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber how these duty shifts were organised and how did -- how long did they last at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to say. There were 12-hour duty shifts at the time from 7.00 to 1900 hours, and from 1900 hours to 0700 hours. It depended on the situation and you would have a smaller number of duty staff and you would have two shifts working.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us the following, for us who are not from the area, with regard to the Opetci village area which is where you were on the 16th and with regard to the village of Zaklopaca, how far are these places in terms of kilometres?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: If you're looking at the area from Miletici, Opetci is to the south and Zaklopaca to the west. The area could be 25 or 30 kilometres from one point to the other. That's a fairly rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your attention has been drawn to paragraph 30 and 31 in your statement. Let's have a look at D659, paragraph 30 and 31. In paragraph 31, you say: "When I arrived in Milici, I found out about this incident and as far as I knew, no one had planned it." Could you please tell the Chamber, where did you arrive in Milici and where did you find out about this incident?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: That evening, as I said, we returned in the early evening hours, dusk, in fact, and I went to the Brkic family because Dragan Brkic is a colleague of mine who was killed on that day as a member of the territorial force and that's what I heard about what had happened in Zaklopaca. Believe me, at that point in time, given everything we had been through, I didn't try to find anything out because we were waiting for people to arrive from the field and it was only 2130, 2200 hours that they went -- that they came out in Derventa and we had a call from Naser, the commander in Srebrenica who asked us if we wanted these two persons or another two persons. There was some kind of black mail here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said on that day, JNA corps were passing through Milici, JNA corps that were withdrawing from Central Bosnia and Croatia. Is the village of Zaklopaca [Realtime transcript read in error "general practitioner"] on the line that was being followed by these JNA units that were withdrawing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Zaklopaca village is right by the main road from Sarajevo to Zvornik. All the former JNA units were withdrawing along that route because that was the only open road to the border with Serbia, so these columns were passing by every day and as a policeman I even escorted some of those columns. On the 15th, the previous day, there was the Tuzla column incident. Part of that unit went who knows where. They were passed by -- they travelled down that route because that was the only open route towards the border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, page 37, line 7, you are recorded as having said is the village of general practitioner, I wonder where there is such a village and could you repeat what you said so that it is known what village you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. For your assistance, I asked about the village of Zaklopaca. And I say this for the sake of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to thank the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to, if everything is fine, thank you once more and I would also like to thank the witness Durmic. Those are all the questions I had, Witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Moloto has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Durmic, P6793 indicated that the report took over at 7.00 in the morning, is that correct? Or do you want to see the exhibit again? Can you call 6793, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Could I have a look at it? I'm not sure what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you see the document before you right now?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you see that it says on this 16th of May, 1992, I took over duty from so and so at 7.00 in the morning. Do you see that? 07?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now bear that number in mind, the time, 7.00 in the morning. Can we now have 6794. Now, on 794, we see it could be 05 or it could be 15. Do you see that? That's what you said, you said it's both. Right, now, if it is 15, would that not be in the same duty duration of the person who came in at 7.00 in the morning? You said the duties were from 7.00 in the morning to 1900 hours.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Well, it's probably the shift of one person because the same person signed this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking you. If it happened if those two incidents happened at 7.00 in the morning, and at 3.00 in the afternoon, they would have been in the same shift, wouldn't they have been? The same shift to 7.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: On that day, we went to the Zutica area, as I was saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You haven't answered my question. Would 7.00 in the morning and 3.00 in the afternoon be in the same shift as 7.00 in the morning to 7.00 in the evening; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: It would, according to what is written here. They would be the same shift.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is all I wanted to find out from you. I'm done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree with me that the report which says that Mr. Bacic Milan started his duty at 7.00 in the morning, that it doesn't say when he gave over his duty to the next person?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes. But could I clarify something, Your Honour? The following who takes over --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can clarify facts, nothing else, fact known to you personally. So if it's about the interpretation of this document, we leave that to the parties and to the Chamber. But if you have anything to add which is within your factual knowledge, you may tell us.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: I wanted to say what common practice was. If I received a report in the morning at 7.00, I make a note of the fact that the person who receives the report from me, whether it's at 1500 hours or 1900 hours, he makes a note of the fact that he took over shift at 1900 hours from such and such a person. That is what I wanted to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently on this day, would you agree with me that the normal shifts did not function because I think whether we start at 05 or at 15 o'clock in the afternoon, it went on until 2300 hours. Which means that the usual shifts apparently did not apply that day. Would you agree or would you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know when this shift took place. I couldn't comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you explained to us whatever you see and what you consider important on the basis of these documents but apparently here you are hesitant to draw any conclusions which is fully appreciated and accepted. Mr. MacDonald, no further questions, if I understand your body language well. This, then, Witness, concludes your evidence. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a very long way to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you unless Mr. Stojanovic, the questions by the Bench have triggered any further need for questions. No. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and having answered all the questions and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so, Your Honour. The witness, I believe, has already arrived. Should I start now or should I start after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think it's another 15 minutes until the break so therefore perhaps you could start already.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Then I suggest that we call Witness Djordjo Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, since the usher is still outside, I'd like to briefly move into private session and when the usher comes in, I'll invite him to bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you. I'd like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, witness, please be seated. Mr. Krstic, at least I assume that you are Mr. Krstic. You'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You'll find Mr. Stojanovic to your left. And Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Krstic.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please slowly tell us your first and last name?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: My name is Djordjo Krstic. Is there anything else I should say?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber whether at one point in time you answered questions put to you in written form by the Mladic Defence team and did you provide a written statement too?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please see the following document in e-court. It's a 65 ter document and the number is 1D01746.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krstic, this is your first time at the Tribunal in The Hague; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In front of you, you can see on the left-hand side of the screen a statement and a signature. Is this your signature and are these details correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now could we have a look at the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You can now see the last page of your statement in front of you. Is this your signature and is this the correct date?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krstic, when you gave -- having given the solemn declaration in this courtroom, would you now answer the questions that were put to you for this statement in the same way? So if you are to now answer the same questions that you answered in your statement, would you provide identical answers to those questions?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like to suggest that 1D01746 which is Mr. Krstic's statement be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D01746 receives number D664.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D664 is admitted. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, I would now like to read the summary of the witness's statement. Djordjo Krstic's statement in which he says that after he had been released for imprisonment by the Green Berets in Sarajevo and following the well known incidents in Dobrovoljacka Street, he joined the VRS as an active soldier from BiH. Up until January 1993, he was engaged in the SRK, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps command and was then transferred to the Eastern Bosnian Corps in Bijeljina, where he was assigned the duties of general affairs officer as well as the deputy warden of the collection centre in Batkovici. He remained at this post until April 1994 when he joined the military police battalion of the Eastern Bosnian Corps which is where he remained until the end of the war. He spoke about the duties he had to perform in the Batkovici collection centre as well as about the gender and age of the prisoners. And he also spoke about the status of those who were brought to the collection centre by the military police unit who had captured them. He also addressed the issue of the accommodation provided for the prisoners and the issue of their personal hygiene. The prisoners were provided with three meals a day. These meals were prepared in the Bijeljina barracks and the food that they were provided with was the same food that members of the VRS were provided with, whereas the water was obtained from the city water supply system and was drinkable. The International Red Cross would visit the prisoners twice a week and the superior command did not obstruct them from having contact with the prisoners, on the contrary, they strove to maintain and promote such cooperation with the International Red Cross. At the same time, representatives of the International Red Cross made or transferred suggestions or made comments that they would submit to the management of the centre if they heard such suggestions made by the prisoners. Prisoners were sent to work within the centre or outside the centre on a voluntary basis and the prisoners were detained in the centre until their status was determined and until a solution was found for them in the form of an exchange or until they were handed over to the International Red Cross who would then send them to the places that they wanted to live in. In his statement, he described how the guard duty was organised and what sort of medical protection was provided for the prisoners. That is the summary, Your Honours, and I would just have a few questions for this witness after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time do you think you would need, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I will need no more than ten minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then those ten minutes can be used after the break. We take a break and the witness is invited to follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can we please have in e-court document D664, and let us focus on paragraph 17 of the statement. 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krstic, you can again see in front of you your statement and in paragraph 17, you describe the procedure when the detainees are being sent to perform labour and you say "the guards shift leader would approach the representative of the prisoners, who was always designated by the prisoners themselves." Please, can you tell me how this process evolved in terms of designating the representatives of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: The procedure was as I described it. At the request of someone or something that came from the command requesting, for example, ten labourers, the guard or somebody from the administration of the centre would approach the man who was one of them, one of the detainees, and he would select --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, your question, if I understood it well, was not about how prisoners of war are chosen but how the representative -- then you should intervene at that moment. Because the witness then starts answering a totally different question. You were asked how the representative of the prisoners was designated by themselves, what the process was in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat my question. Please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I repeated the question already. Could you tell us the process of designating a representative by the prisoners. How did that work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The prisoners themselves would elect their representatives from among themselves a person who would be suitable for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While you were performing the deputy duties, was that always the same person or was there an alternate selection?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Well, mainly it was one and the same person but there was some replacements if it happened that the original one was exchanged or sent elsewhere in a different manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was it always the same person, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want me to give you the name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't remember the name of that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the only thing we've learned until now is that where the witness in his statement says that the representative was designated by the prisoners, that we now know that he was elected by the prisoners which is not much of a difference. So therefore I, wonder what the question was about at all. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 19 of your statement, you speak about two different kinds of security and you distinguish between the internal and the external security. Can you tell the Chamber who was in charge of external security, of those people?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: These people would come in shifts from other units. They did not have permanent residence in the collection centre but rather a unit would designate about 20-odd people to perform the guard duty and to secure the external perimeter of the compound and they were replaced every seven days, which means that not always one and the same unit provided them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
