utterances.text: And who was in charge of the internal security guards?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: The internal security guards were people from the military police battalion of the Eastern Bosnia Corps however there were only three of them who took shifts whether on a weekly basis or on a different period of replacement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djordjo, at this point, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, again the last question is already answered in the statement of the witness so therefore there was no need whatsoever to put that question to the witness again. And by the way, we received the same answer. Ms. Bibles, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krstic, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Bibles. Ms. Bibles is counsel for the Prosecution and you'll find her to your right. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Krstic.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could have D47 on our screens, please, we can go to page 1 in both versions. Sir, the document coming up on the screen is an indictment from the district court of Bijeljina. We see four accused described here. And my question is whether number 3 in this list is you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Turning to page 2 now in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We see that you're listed as the deputy camp warden in the collection centre in Batkovic and later on this page, I believe we see -- it's actually towards the top third of the page, we see that the time period is listed as 11 January 1993 to 6 June of 1994. Does this correspond to the dates that you were the deputy camp commander at Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Is this the situation that you're describing in paragraph 20 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Are you currently on trial for these charges?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And these relate to charges which include violating the rules of the International Law of War, the ordering of murders, causing of great physical or mental pain or suffering, violence to life and persons and inhumane treatment?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, is a Rule 90(E) issue perhaps -- Witness, I'd like to inform you about the content of one of the Rules before this Court and I'll read it slowly to you. A witness, so at this moment that's you, may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate that witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony. Now, let me further explain to you. If you have concerns that any truthful answer might tend to incriminate yourself, you may address me and you may object to answering that question. We'll then consider whether or not we'll compel you to do so. But if you would be compelled to answer the question, and again I'm saying that we would carefully consider whether at all we would even consider to compel you to do so, that if you then answer that question, the answer could not be used against yourself but it could be used against yourself if the answer would not be in accordance with the truth and you would expose yourself to being prosecuted for perjury. I'd like to explain to you that the same is true for the written statements. If there's anything in that statement which is not true and which you -- the answers you may have given in order to protect yourself against any incrimination, then you better would tell us now rather than at any later moment because you expose yourself to being prosecuted for perjury if there's anything in those statements which is not in accordance with the truth. So I'm explaining this to you that this applies both for answers to questions still to be put to you, but it may also apply, although you have given the statement already and you've confirmed it already, that if you have given any untrue statement until now, that you expose yourself to being prosecuted for perjury. Now, in this Tribunal, the maximum penalty for perjury is seven years of imprisonment and/or a fine of a considerable amount. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Completely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both in relation to what you have stated already and in relation to what you are still about to testify about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could now see 65 ter 31357 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, I'll now be directing a number of questions towards the time period when you first arrived at Batkovic and what you observed. This document that we see on the screen is a 4 August 1992 order from Colonel Ilic ordering an adaption of the camp to make a second building for holding prisoners. When you arrived at Batkovic in January of 1993, how many buildings held detainees at that time?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: When I came there, there were two buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 of your statement, you describe that there were 1700 detainees when you arrived. Can you tell us how many people were in each of the two structures?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: I said approximately 1700. I cannot give you 100 per cent accurate figure. That's how it was during that period. So roughly speaking half of them were in one building and the other half was in the other building. I cannot give you the exact number though.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Turning our attention to item 3 in this order, we see direction to prepare the camp for foreign journalists and the International Red Cross. Didn't you receive similar orders to this one before International Red Cross visits?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this order is from 1992 and I wasn't there at the time. I don't remember this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, my question is didn't you receive similar orders advising you that the International Red Cross and perhaps journalists were coming and that you should prepare the camp?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: We didn't receive any specific order. That was the usual practice to keep everything in order. No particular preparations were made for either the journalists or the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender 31357.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31357 receives number P6795, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 of your statement sets out that you were assigned to serve as deputy manager of Batkovic immediately after you were transferred to the East Bosnia Corps. Who assigned you to serve there?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: The command of the Eastern Bosnia Corps and they issued an official written document to that effect assigning me to that post.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Where did you reside while you were serving as deputy manager of Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: In one of the buildings where the detainees were, there was separate rooms which we used as offices so in one of the two buildings where the detainees were held.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you reside there throughout 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, during the period that I stated concerning the duty that I was performing. If you are referring to this period, I don't know if you had something else in mind, for example, how many hours during the day I spent there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In paragraph 6, you mention that the checks of persons taken to the collection centre in Batkovic for various reasons were performed by the security organs of the corps command, the military prosecution, and organs in charge of such checks. The corps command was the East Bosnia Corps command; right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: What other organs were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: The military police organs and the prosecution. Nobody else, because they were part of the Eastern Bosnia Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: After checks were performed, the Batkovic staff provided information to the East Bosnia Corps command about who was being detained; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: I suppose so. I wasn't in charge of reviewing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 of your statement, you advise that when you came to Batkovic, the 1700 prisoners were from all over Bosnia and Herzegovina. This suggests that you were briefed as to where these detainees had come from; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: What kind of briefing did you receive about Batkovic when you took the assignment there?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question, what do you mean "briefing"? If you can be more specific, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Who provided information to you about the current status of Batkovic when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: The warden whose deputy I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: What was that individual's name when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Djoko Pajic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: It's true that the majority of the prisoners were non-Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes. But there were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: The vast majority of the detainees at Batkovic were non-Serbs, however; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you know, when you arrived, that Batkovic held prisoners who had been transferred from Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could have P3990 on our screens, please, page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, as this comes up, this is an article by Elie Wiesel published by the Guardian which is a British newspaper and it's dated the 1st of March, 1993. Beginning on page 1 down towards the bottom, we see a discussion of the journalist's visit to the prisoners at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And then if we could move to the end of page 2 in both versions. We read: "Shortly after our visit, that camp," referring to Manjaca "was closed in our honour, as Karadzic put in a letter to an Italian journalist. So far so good. Better yet, all the prisoners from Manjaca were said to have been handed over to the International Committee of the Red Cross but last month there came terrible news, not all the prisoners had been freed. Some 500 remained unaccounted for. Most disturbing to me was that many of those I had interviewed had been singled out for special punishment and transferred to an even worse camp, Batkovic." Sir, is it true that the men from Manjaca were treated more harshly than the other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: That's not true. They were treated like everybody else and in addition to that, they stayed for a short period of time. According to the information I have, they remained there simply because there were some technical problems, of which I know nothing, that occurred during the exchange and their handing over to the International Red Cross so they were temporarily accommodated with us, as far as I recollect. They did not come there as punishment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, we -- would you agree that we were talking about over 500 men who had been held at Manjaca who arrived at Batkovic when you were there in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was it one year after or was it in March of 1993? He came in January. So these people must have come there while he was there already.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'll follow up with some questions about, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, did these men from Manjaca come to Batkovic while you were there?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And how many men are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact number but roughly 500, but I'm not 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 7052 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, this is a 14 December 1992 report to the 1st Krajina Corps command from Manjaca camp. And this is describing events as the camp closed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could first look at the end of the page where we see a list of the journalists and I believe this is in both versions. And perhaps it's on the next page in the B/C/S version. Yes. The top of the next page there in B/C/S. The line that's underlined.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We see: "It is also characteristic that the ICRC delegates were interested in a group of prisoners who were exchanged yesterday. They asked a few times whether we as the camp command knew the outcome of the exchange. We also heard from several sources that the Croatian radio broadcast the news at 6 in the morning, 0600 in the morning, that yesterday 520 prisoners mainly Croats --"

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: " -- from taken away from the "notorious Serbo-Chetnik Manjaca camp" to an unknown location to be exchanged." Sir, aren't these the 520 men who were actually taken to Batkovic rather than exchanged?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: It's possible. It's possible. But I can't have a clear idea of what this is about on the basis of this letter but I assume it's the 500 men. They did arrive in our camp but they didn't stay long. They were soon exchanged and sent to the Zemunik area near Zadar, near the airport. Ten of them returned because they didn't want to cross over to the other side. We had exchanges at the lines and they decided not to go through with the exchange and returned with us to Bijeljina again. I can't tell you about the dates but this happened sooner after their departure from Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, first I would tender 7052.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 7052 receives number P6796, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If can he could next go to P3992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, as the document comes up, you'll see that this is a East Bosnia Corps letter regarding prisoners who had arrived at Batkovic from Manjaca. Sir, are these the individuals that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this. This is 1992. I wasn't there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could now go to 3887, please. I'm sorry P3887, not 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, this is an ICRC press communique dated 18 December 1992. If we look at the third paragraph down you'll note that the press release or the press communique indicates Manjaca has been closed down but quoting the third paragraph: "In another development, during a visit to a camp in Batkovic, in north-east Bosnia, delegates found some of the 529 detainees who had been transferred from Manjaca on 13 December without the ICRC's knowledge. A visit to this camp is currently underway." Sir, when you talked about prisoners coming from Manjaca, the 500 or so prisoners, are these the prisoners, the 529 or so that the ICRC had not been advised of?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Prisoners were often taken to the camp, so I cannot remember where many of them came from, when. As for those I was speaking about a while ago, whether they were from somewhere else, well, I can't connect this. I know those that came from Manjaca to our camp stayed there for a very short period of time, not even a month, I think. And most of them were exchanged either through the -- or they went to third countries through the ICRC. That's what I can remember about the process at the time because the period was a chaotic one and it was difficult to find one's bearings in that chaos.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: But sir, you've confirmed that there were about 500 prisoners from Manjaca who you recall at Batkovic, and we've seen information that 500 in December of 1992 came to Batkovic from Manjaca. And is it your testimony now that you're not sure if you were dealing in January of 1993 with a different 500 prisoners from Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: At the top it says January 1992, as far as I can see. In January 1993, there was no one in the camp in Batkovici. I said that prisoners were taken there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we verify whether the witness has the right document before him because on our screens, Witness, it reads communication to the press No. 92/37, 18 December 1992. Is that what you have in front of you as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we will then ignore that you said that it was about January 1993. Or did the witness say January 1992? Let's just have a look.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor said 1993 and that's why I said that that wasn't the case in 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, page 60, the witness said that in January 1993 there was no one from the camp in Manjaca in Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received such interpretation, in December 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: So, sir, there seems to be some confusion. When I first started asking questions about prisoners from Manjaca and reviewed the article in the British news about prisoners from Manjaca, you agreed that there were prisoners from Manjaca while you were there and you agreed that it was about 500. Are we talking about a different group?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: I arrived in January 1993 and at the time there were some prisoners whom I saw there and probably some of them had been brought in from Manjaca or from somewhere else, I couldn't say. But in 1993, there were Croats who were brought in, prisoners of Croatian ethnicity. They were escorted there from Manjaca. They didn't stay long in our camp and they were exchanged in the Zadar area near the Zemunik airport. If you have understood what I want to say now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: So, trying to understand the sequence. We have seen documents that indicate that Manjaca was closed in December of 1992 and that 500 -- over 500 prisoners were taken to Batkovic. Your testimony is that there may have been some of those present in Manjaca in January of 1993 but that in 1993, Croats were brought in from Manjaca and that they were later exchanged. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: I haven't understood your question again. You keep referring to January 1993, yes, January 1993. Yes, yes, that's correct. I got a little confused with the dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: So you do recall prisoners of a Croat ethnicity coming to Batkovic in 1993 from Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We'll shift directions in the questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I nevertheless ask a question. The approximate number of prisoners of Croat ethnicity who were coming in 1993 from Manjaca, when -- how many approximately were there who arrived, those Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say exactly, but about 500 or so. But I can't remember the exact figure. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are puzzled by the following: Information exists that Manjaca closed down in December 1992. Now, it is for us difficult to understand how nevertheless, 500 Croats could arrive from Manjaca in January 1993. Or at least somewhere in early 1993 and we are wondering whether not in one way or another, you are mixing up a number of 500 prisoners coming from Manjaca in December with those as you said 500 Croats who arrived in 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible. Let me clarify this. When I arrived there, there were a lot of people already in the camp. Where they came from, I didn't know at the time. Perhaps there was a group that arrived before I arrived in the camp but I do remember those Croats and I escorted -- I was part of the escort and I was part of the commission when they were exchanged in Zemunik. So there were groups that would arrive, but as for the dates and so on, I can't remember all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you're focussing now on when they left Batkovic rather than when they arrived. That group of Croats, did they arrive when you were there already?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, as far as I could remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that would mean that, apart from the 500 reported to have transferred to Batkovic in December 1992, that there was another group of 500 arriving in 1993 which make a total of approximately 1.000 prisoners coming from Manjaca arriving in Batkovic of which you said 500 were Croats.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said when I was there, the Croats arrived but these people arrived before I went there, perhaps it was about 500 or so, that could be the figure, but I'm not sure. I wasn't there. As for whether they were from Manjaca or not, that is information I do not have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have one additional question in this respect. What was the status of those who arrived from Manjaca? Were they all combatants or really prisoners of war or was there a possibility that there were civilians among them as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know much about the status, whether they were combatants or had some other status. According to the information I had, they were detained there temporarily at the time because no technical arrangements had been made for exchanges so they weren't there for very long. It was as if they were waiting for things to be organised, for an exchange to be organised. There were certain problems as far as that is concerned. I think it had to do with whether they should be exchanged in Zemunik or somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you do not know whether you were detaining civilians at that point in time even for a short period.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. No, I don't have that information. We didn't look into that for the people who came from Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You didn't verify the status of those coming from Manjaca, whether they were prisoners of war or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my opinion, they were prisoners of war. That's what I was told. But as to what they were, well, it wasn't my role to look into or verify what their status was. The security organs had that task and that is what I said in my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But they were detained under your authority, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, under my authority when it comes to providing security, food and so on and so forth, other necessities. But they weren't under my authority in the sense that I was to verify certain matters or launch investigations into things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But also under your authority, they were kept within the perimeter of the camp which they couldn't leave because they were guarded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm again informing you that if truthful answers would incriminate yourself, that you may object to answer such a question because keeping civilians in detention, not caring about whether they're prisoners of war may be, if you state about that, may be, to some extent, incriminate yourself. I again bring this to your attention and I leave it now to Ms. Bibles to continue her cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree that there were some individuals that the military police brought to Batkovic that Batkovic took responsibility for but placed for detention somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that. Whoever was taken there by the military police stayed there in our camp and they didn't go anywhere else until an exchange was organised or some other solution was found.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 31358 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, I also refer to the fact that in paragraph 6 of your statement, you said that there were never women and children in Batkovic. First I want to clarify that you meant that there were no women or children in Batkovic after January of 1993. Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, now on our screens, we see a 12 February 1993 referral signed by Colonel Gavric sending nine women to KPD in Bijeljina because they can't be held in Batkovic. To be clear, sending these women to KPD meant that they were to be held in a prison facility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: KPD has nothing to do with us. It was a civilian institution, the courts had authority over it as well as the civilian police so it had absolutely nothing to do with the army and this document also has nothing to do with us. The KPD was a separate thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, let's go back to my question. First, would you agree that KPD was a prison, as you pointed out, a civilian prison?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: You would agree that this document is signed by Colonel Gavric of the Eastern Bosnia Corps command?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And in this document, it indicates that these nine women were brought from Zvornik to Batkovic. You see that in the document?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, you see just above the signature where the Colonel writes, "The collection centre will take responsibility for providing their meals and other needs." Wouldn't you agree that Batkovic collection centre was maintaining responsibility for these women?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, looking at the names on the list, I would ask you if you would agree that these women are non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And I'd ask you to look at the date of birth for the women listed as numbers 8 and 9 on the list, both reflect that they were born in 1918. Would you agree that they would have been 75 years of age in 1993?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you know anything about what happened to these women either during or after their time in KPD in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about them. I'm not at all familiar with this event.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender 31358.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, I just want to -- Mr. Krstic, you realise the date of this document is the 12th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By that time, you were at Batkovic as a deputy warden, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When they came there to Batkovic, you must have been -- that's during your term of office there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Isn't it surprising --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They didn't go to Batkovic. I know nothing about those people or rather about the women on this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This -- the report says "They were brought from Zvornik to the Batkovic collection centre. The proper conditions are not in place for women to stay at the Batkovic collection centre." You should be aware of them coming there whether or not they stayed there for any length of time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me say perhaps this occurred when I was absent from the camp. I wasn't there every day. Sometimes I had a day off so perhaps the warden of the Batkovic camp was there. But I don't remember that and no one told me about the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Perhaps they might have also have come while you were there as opposed to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of any women being taken there. I didn't see any women.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear you say you're not aware but perhaps they might have come while you were there in as much as it is quite possible they could have come when you were not there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This isn't something that I am familiar with. That's why I'm saying I know nothing about it. I didn't see anyone. I know nothing about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You may proceed, Madam Bibles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but one further. Witness, if you say there had never been any women, children or elderly persons, I now do understand that you meant to say I am not aware of any women, children or elderly persons having been in Batkovic. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, do we have to understand all the rest of your statement in a similar way, that is, where you say this did not happen or that did happen that it's always as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd like to return to the questions about civilians being held at Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I would like if we could have 65 ter 25955 on our screens, please. Oh, I'm sorry. I can't remember if I've tendered this document or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You haven't tendered it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I would do so now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31358 receives number P6797, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'd now ask if we could have 65 ter 25955 on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, this is an order from General Milovanovic, it's dated 16 July 1993. I direct your attention as it comes up to the first paragraph of this order. You see under the word "order", and then under the number one: "Transfer all soldiers and civilians who are now in the prisons in your zone of responsibility to the Batkovic collection camp in Bijeljina." Sir, wouldn't you agree this makes it clear that civilians were being held in other facilities as well and at least in this instance brought to Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: In my statement, I also said that I didn't know who was a civilian and who was a soldier. In my view, they were all prisoners and they were all of military age. As for whether -- who was the civilian or who was a soldier was the matter that the military police dealt with and the people who were brought under this order, I also had no information about who amongst them were civilians and who were members of the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: But certainly you knew that among the people being held prisoner were civilians.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: I never gave it a thought. That was not my job to ponder whether somebody was a civilian or a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Following this order, where as we see in this order the implementation that is bringing all the civilians and soldiers to Batkovic was to take place by the 22nd of July 1993. Can you tell us how many such individuals were brought to Batkovic between the 16th of July and the 22nd of July of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot remember the people were being brought from Zvornik, even Samac, therefore I cannot recall the exact number. All I know is that people had been brought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it by the tens? Was it by the hundreds? Was it just a few individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would say around 100. That would be a rough figure. But I cannot confirm that with 100 per cent surety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you I would tender 25955.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 25955 receives number P6798, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And I'll shift directions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, could you tell us how much more time you'd approximately need?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Looks like about ten minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, we lost half an hour this morning. Is there any objection by the Defence to continue for another ten minutes and then to adjourn for the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In paragraph 17 of your statement, you indicate that prisoners were sent to work outside the camp on a voluntary basis. And today, at transcript page 47, lines 11 through -2, you gave additional information which is that the request for such workers would come in from I believe you said command. The Trial Chamber has received evidence that in March of 1993, detainees from Batkovic were forced to dig trenches for Serbs at the front lines in the area of Lopar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could have P3970 on our screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, as this comes on the screen you'll see that it's an ICRC press communique dated 2 April 1993. This was during your time at Batkovic. We read in the first paragraph that ICRC learned: "17 detainees might have lost their lives on 26 March when the vehicle transporting them to the front line was ambushed." And sir, the Chamber has received evidence that this did in fact occur. My question to you, sir, is did you take any steps to stop the use of detainees at the front lines either before or after this event?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware of the event, it did not take place on the front line but in the vicinity of the front line, there were felling trees for the centre. They were ambushed and they did what they did. We were not able to undertake any other measures except for providing guards with them who also became victims as they did. And while I was there, they were never performing any labour on the front line itself, and I'm talking about the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you take any steps to try to prohibit detainees from being taken to, as you call it, the vicinity of the front line?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes. They never went close to the front line again, not even further away. There was a large distance between their place of work and the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, could I seek one clarifying question. You said as far as you're aware of the event, it did not take place on the front line but in the vicinity. At what distance from the front line were they doing their job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as I can judge, it might have been between seven and eight kilometres, roughly speaking. I cannot tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So they were far away from the front line. They're not even in the vicinity. It is at a considerable distance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You nevertheless then decided that they never went close to the front line again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you put them at 10, 15, 20 kilometres from the front line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They never went outside Bijeljina. They remained within the town limits of Bijeljina which was considerably far from the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Cutting trees in town, is that what they did there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I was talking about the group who were the victims and what happened, happened. After that, they never went again to cut trees. Instead, we opted for acquiring coal from the mine and this work was provided by the regular mine workers, not by the detainees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We'll need to go into private session, actually, for the next question.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, I have two final questions. If we could go to P345 and we'll look at page 87 in the English and page 89 in the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: While these are coming up, sir, I'll ask if you recall meeting with General Mladic on the 13th of April, 1995?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: What meeting are you talking about? I never attended a meeting with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir -- we're looking at notebooks of General Mladic and at the top of the page, we see the 13th of April, 1995. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you see your name?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: But that is not my name. I was not the only Djordje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, it's a very quick response that it's not your name. It seems to be your name but you're not certain yet as to whether it refers to you or by another person with the same name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my name but whether it's a different person, I cannot confirm that. But I never had any meeting with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you have a meeting with the parents of prisoners on the 13th of April, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wasn't in Batkovic at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that it was in Batkovic. Did you have a meeting with the parents of prisoners in April 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just follow up. Sir, did you say the man who used to take people away from Batkovic was Vojkan somebody, what was his surname again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no Vojkan taking people away, but if you are referring to the Vojkan previously mentioned his last name is Djurkovic. However he never came to Batkovic, or at least I never saw him there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you were being asked in the context of him taking people and I see here he's mentioned by the first name but he takes people away in their socks. Unless I misheard Madam Bibles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He never came. The Vojkan whom I knew by sight only, he never came to Batkovic for any reason whatsoever. At least, I never saw him. Whether he came through some other channels unbeknownst to me, that's a different thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one further question. Could you tell us whether there was any Djordje Krstic in Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a man in Bijeljina named Djordje Krstic but he was a local of that place. I know him by sight also but we are not related in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he ever appear in Batkovic as far as you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Djordje Krstic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what and when.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, my question is whether this Djordje Krstic as you said who lived in Bijeljina was he ever in Batkovic camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not to my knowledge. This man never appeared there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I put it to you that the Djordje Krstic who is described here apparently has knowledge of the ordering of the expulsion of Muslims, an opinion which he expressed in a meeting with the parents of prisoners. Do you have any explanation as what other Djordje Krstic could have been referred to in this context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't in that meeting. Whether this other Djordje was there, I cannot say. I only know him by sight. I know nothing else about him. What he was doing, what his role in Bijeljina was as far as I know, he had been living in Bijeljina since before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we have to adjourn for the day because the teams are needed for the Hadzic case. Mr. Stojanovic, would you have any further questions? I'm not allowing you to put them to the witness now but could you give us some indication as to how long you would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, with your leave I would only have one question and then we can finish with this witness if you think that is sufficient, then I'm all right with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Experience tells me that one question from you sometimes amounts to three, four or five. If it's really one, I will allow you to put that question to the witness but I'll limit you then to one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. If it was going to be a leading question, please prevent me from putting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krstic, you mentioned a person called Djordje Krstic. My question is do you know if this Djordje Krstic aka Djojo [phoen] married to Mara has a son, Miljan Krstic, who was taken prisoner at Lisic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJO KRSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the Djordje Krstic I was referring to according to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for the day, Ms. Bibles. If you would have any further questions I'll not allow you to put them to the witness now but please indicate whether you want to further explore the matter which came up in the last question and whether you want to -- or would you --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have no re-cross following that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague for and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, the 30th of September in this same courtroom III at 9.00 in the morning, not later. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 30th day of September, 2014 at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
